title: FluxGuard: A Haptic Flux-Sensing Wristband that Warns and Steers Substation Workers Away from Lethal Induction
content: High-voltage substations are threaded with invisible, time-varying magnetic flux. The body has no sense organ for it. Unlike heat or noise, the field gives a worker no natural warning at all until induced currents are already stimulating nerve and heart tissue. (1) Background: the personal protective equipment issued today says nothing about field exposure, and the single-sensor proximity alarms that do exist suffer from blind spots and saturation at exactly the field levels that matter. This raises a practical question: can a wrist-worn device catch hazardous power-frequency fields early, keep working when parts of it fail, and steer a frightened wearer to safety without asking them to think? (2) Methods: we present FluxGuard, a lightweight wristband that watches for hazardous fields using five independent detection methods running in parallel. These are a three-axis induction-coil sensor (Faraday’s law), a wide-range Hall-effect magnetometer (Lorentz force), a capacitive electricfield probe (displacement current), a tunnelling-magnetoresistive (TMR) bridge (spin-dependent tunnelling), and an ultrasonic corona listener (acoustic partial discharge). Their verdicts are fused by first-detect-wins (1-out-of-5 OR) trigger logic, so the slowest channel never delays the fastest. The band also estimates which way the exposure decreases, using a short-baseline gradiometer hardened by three independent bearing estimators under confidence-gated voting. (3) Results: each alert stage is mapped onto the body-current tolerance zones, and even the maximum warning is anchored below the 10mA let-go threshold. Redundant sensing across five distinct physical principles, a continuous self-test, an analog comparator fast path that bypasses the firmware entirely, and a latching fail-safe alarm together make the architecture tolerant of any single sensor, filter, or software fault. A cognition-free guidance suite (withdrawal-reflex lateral haptics, a zero-memory “warmer/colder” closed loop, a world-locked escape arrow, spoken escort commands, and automatic man-down SOS) keeps steering a startled or collapsing wearer, or summons rescue when the wearer can no longer respond. (4) Conclusions: the paper sets out the physical principles, full block and circuit diagrams, and a build guide, and then goes further than a bench prototype: it works through design for manufacture (bill of materials, mixed-signal PCB floor-plan, per-sensor manufacturing constraints, factory calibration, end-of-line safety testing, and the reliability, functional-safety, and regulatory path) and closes with a feasibility-to-integration analysis of embedding the same protection in an ordinary smartphone paired with an external high-flux sensor pod.
